content: If HIV reactivity remains unchanged, individuals will be diagnosed as HIV-negative. According to the 2019 WHO guidelines on HIV testing services, retesting is recommended 14 days after an inconclusive HIV status using the same testing strategy and algorithm. If the reactivity resolves to either HIV-positive (A1+, A2+, A3+) or HIV-negative (A1−), the results should be reported accordingly. Retesting for individuals with inconclusive HIV status should ideally be conducted at the same site using the same testing strategy and algorithm. Key post-test counseling messages for inconclusive and HIV-negative results are outlined in Chapter 4. While most individuals who test HIV-negative do not require frequent retesting, certain populations may need annual or more frequent retesting. Chapters 4 and 7 provide guidance on populations requiring retesting and the associated counseling messages. For individuals initiating pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), HIV testing is mandatory before starting PrEP to confirm HIV-negative status and minimize the risk of developing HIV resistance. Periodic retesting is also recommended for PrEP users to detect breakthrough HIV infections as early as possible. Most individuals who acquire HIV while on PrEP programs are those who have discontinued PrEP. WHO recommends using the same testing strategy and algorithm for PrEP users as for other individuals. Some clinical trials for PrEP initiation have used assays optimized for detecting acute HIV infection during the initial visit. However, more expensive and complex testing strategies are unlikely to provide additional benefits in settings where nucleic acid testing (NAT) or fourth-generation serology assays are not routinely used. For periodic retesting while on PrEP, WHO recommends the same testing strategy and algorithm as for other individuals. Proper adherence to PrEP significantly reduces the risk of HIV acquisition. However, in settings with low HIV testing service (HTS) positivity rates, the likelihood of a false-positive HIV-reactive result increases. Employing a different testing strategy or algorithm may not provide additional benefits given the associated costs and complexity. In cases of inconclusive HIV status, particularly in individuals with clinical signs meeting WHO criteria for stage III or IV HIV infection, the impaired immune system may result in a decreased HIV antibody response. Weekly serology testing for four weeks using the same testing strategy and algorithm is recommended in such cases, as NAT is not expected to detect the virus in the presence of PrEP. If the serology profile remains unchanged (e.g., A1+, A2+, A3− or A1+, A2−), the individual is considered HIV-negative, and PrEP can be continued with quarterly retesting. If the serology profile evolves to A1+, A2+, A3+, the individual is HIV-positive, and the diagnosis must be confirmed before transitioning from PrEP to antiretroviral therapy (ART). This confirmation should involve a different testing provider, preferably at a different site, using new specimens and different assay lots. If the above approach is not feasible, PrEP may be discontinued for up to four weeks, during which weekly serology and virological testing should be performed. This period allows the virus to resume replication and induce an antibody response if present. During this time, alternative HIV prevention methods, such as condoms, should be strongly recommended. NAT assays are unsuitable for periodic testing of PrEP users because antiretroviral drugs suppress viral replication below the detection limit of NAT. The routine testing strategy and algorithm are the most appropriate for quarterly HIV testing in PrEP users. Expanding community-based testing through test-for-triage and HIV self-testing (HIVST) is critical for reaching underserved populations. Test-for-triage involves a trained provider conducting a single HIV rapid diagnostic test (RDT) rather than the full testing algorithm. This approach reduces stigma and simplifies training, enabling broader access to testing. Reactive results from test-for-triage or HIVST require confirmatory testing using the standard WHO testing algorithm. Multiplex testing, which detects multiple analytes, is increasingly used for HIV and other infections. For example, dual HIV/syphilis RDTs are particularly useful in antenatal care (ANC) settings, as they are easy to perform and do not require refrigeration. These tests can detect syphilis antibodies even after successful treatment, making them valuable for increasing testing and treatment coverage. In settings where HIV-2 is documented, supplemental testing, including serology assays specific to HIV-1 and HIV-2 and virological technologies, is necessary to determine the virus type or diagnose co-infection. Cross-reactivity between HIV-1 and HIV-2 in commercially available assays can lead to incorrect diagnoses, highlighting the need for careful assay selection. Testing strategies should prioritize products with high sensitivity for Assay 1 to rule in all HIV-positive individuals, even if this results in some false-reactive results. Assays 2 and 3 should have higher specificity to rule out false-reactive results. Other factors, such as stability, time to result, and ease of use, should also influence product selection.
